### [Ways into the Cathedral - an Address from Rev Child](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/ways-into-the-cathedral-an-address-from-rev-child)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 11, 2026

I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let us go to the house of the Lord!’ (Psalm 122:1) We’ve been in the cathedral a fair bit since term started. I want to start with a question for you to think about, whether you’re new here or whether you’ve been around for a while: How many different ways into the cathedral do you think there are? When you came in this morning, you had a choice of two doorways – the two west corners at the back. On the first day of term, for a bit of pomp and ceremony, we opened the main west doors to allow a procession in and out. There are other ways in through the gift shop; or through the north or south transepts. All the way up at the east end there’s a door that leads from Edith Cavell’s grave outside to the inside of the military chapel. There used to be a suspended walkway from upstairs in the Bishop’s Palace across to the first floor level in here to save the bishop getting rained on. I’m actually not sure myself how many ways into Norwich Cathedral there are now. If you know the answer – or if at some point you have a spare ten minutes to walk round the building counting the doorways – perhaps you could let me know. Many years ago, before I lived and worked in Norwich, before I was even a priest, I visited Norwich Cathedral with a group of year 6 children from South London. They were in Norfolk on their week-long school journey to experience something different to their usual. I don’t remember which door we came in that day. But I do remember that I was a bit concerned about one of the pupils in the group. His name was Daniel. He was the naughty one. I was worried he was going to find the cathedral boring and start messing around. As it turned out, I was completely wrong. We started our tour in the cloisters – the outdoors space on the south side surrounded by walkways and pillars. Our guide was a retired teacher who guessed that, before we saw the stained glass windows or the bishop’s cathedra, we might like to see a game played by the monks who originally lived here. It was a very simple game – the monks would stand on the ledges in the cloisters and swing round the pillars like apes. (We know that they did this because their feet wore grooves into the stone that you can still see today.) Our guide had already spotted Daniel, and he asked him to demonstrate swinging round the pillars. Sure enough, Daniel’s feet naturally fitted into the grooves as he moved. From that moment, he was fascinated. I think partly because he simply wasn’t expecting there to be fun in the cathedral. But with the help of the guide, Daniel found his own way into this place. Later we were shown some hidden medieval graffiti. Right in the middle of it we happened to find Daniel’s initials, carved by someone centuries ago. It was wonderful to watch Daniel feeling like he belonged here. However many literal doorways there are, I hope you can all find your own figurative way into this cathedral. If you have some kind of a maths brain, the physics and the proportions around us are extraordinary. A while ago Dr Leeder gave an assembly on how many Smarties you can fit in this space. Let the numbers inspire you. If you’re someone who likes Art and Design, there’s no shortage of craftmanship in here that you can get up close to. It’s not all in the past; even today you might see a modern stonemason winching a block of stone up the scaffolding outside to repair centuries of rain and wind erosion. Be inspired by the necessary work of people who are really good at 3D Design. If you’ve just started a course in Psychology, ask yourself why human beings are motivated to begin buildings like this in the first place. The first ever Bishop of Norwich, buried at the east end, was consumed by shame and guilt; he began the construction of this cathedral as a penance. Just about everything we teach is represented: languages, like Latin and a little Anglo-Norman; or poetry, written on the walls; or music, of course; or history, in bucketloads. It’s all here, waiting for you to spot something that catches your interest, and which will take you further in. What is generally true in education is true here: there are many ways in. Just choose your doorway. I want to close by reading part of an email that I got from an ON recently. This is someone who has been away from Norwich School for two decades and now lives in Australia; these are his recollections. Looking back, it is quite remarkable that a load of teenagers meet in the cathedral in the morning… I barely noticed how unusual this was at the time, but the very act of starting the day within an enormous, time-tested cathedral and singing together has by itself a very unifying and edifying effect. When catching up with my peers occasionally, one repeated theme that emerges is how we miss the sense of the transcendent that pervaded school life in the cathedral close. It's so easy to become busied up with urban life and work… longing for meaning and fullness and forgetting where it comes from. You may know that on this date 25 years ago – the 11th September 2001, or 9/11 – there was an attack on the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon in Washington which sent shock waves around the globe. We keep this anniversary in mind as we come to our prayer for this morning, which is the Benedictine Prayer for Peace. Benedictine prayer for peace We would like to be people of peace; to walk the paths of peace our whole life long, and to lead others into the ways of peace. May there be peace in our hearts, peace in our homes, peace in our sorely troubled world. May we be peace-makers, ready to take the first step in ending bitterness, being the first to hold out our hands in friendship and forgiveness. May peace, grace and love permeate our daily living. In the fullness of time, may we know the reward of being peacemakers.

By Eleanor Lewis•September 9, 2026

I'm wearing my Make America Great Again hats today and you will be forming an opinion of what that represents. Costume is very powerful, and a MAGA hat is almost like a flag. I don't know, I must try to be balanced, and there might be Donald Trump fans in your family. In social situations, I signal my hostility to MAGA with a frown. Can I recommend that to you? When you are part of a conversation that you know is unkind, don't be a bystander. Very often a frown is a powerful and effective response that sends a very clear signal without provoking a bigger argument. It’s called frown power. Maybe we should put the ‘Great’ back into Britain. That’s a gentle joke on the people who say that sort of thing, since it indicates that they don't know what Great Britain means. Excuse me a moment while I explain. There is a large group of about 150 inhabited islands off the coast of northwestern Europe. Collectively they are called the British Isles. There are two big ones: the one on the left(west) is called Ireland. The one on the right is called Great Britain, because it is the biggest of the British Isles. This morning you are resident in a country called the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Great Britain isn't going to stop being Great anytime soon. My assembly today aims to encourage you to imagine an even better Britain: not by looking back into an imagined past, but to inspire you to work towards a future version that's even better than the present, or the past. Today I have a dreadful story to tell you about a disaster in Wales that took place almost exactly 60 years ago. Just because quite a lot of things are bad now, it doesn’t mean that everything is getting worse, or that things used to better. Things that are normal today: health and safety, counselling, accountability, litigation, compensation – were almost completely absent 60 years ago. I’m 56, so while 60 years ago sounds like ancient history if you are 12, it isn’t all that long ago in reality. On that dreadful day in October 1966, it had been raining hard for weeks. The 240 pupils of the Aberfan Junior School wound their way through the back lanes of miners’ terrace houses on their way to morning assembly. You probably know that coal mining built industrial Britain. But by 1966, the coal industry had been in long decline and several pits had shut. The mining workforce had fallen from its peak, but pit jobs kept Aberfan going. The National Coal Board had control of UK mining and wielded great power. It had a firm grip on government, and it was held in what now seems uncomfortable reverence. The working man knew his place; authority knew best. Numerous complaints had been made to the Coal Board about the dangers of one of the seven gigantic spoil tips that loomed high above the village. Every mining community had its tips of waste material dug from the mines. The entire south Wales valleys landscape was jagged with them. The one above Aberfan had slipped three years previously when an ominous crater appeared at the top. A bulge had formed at the foot of the tip as a stream that was unable to drain away liquefied the tip into thick, black quicksand. The Coal Board brushed the complaints aside. Everyone knew that if they made a fuss, the mine would be closed. If the disaster had come 20 minutes earlier, the junior school below the tip would have been empty. In the classrooms lights began to flicker and sway before there was an ominous roar. A glistening black avalanche consumed everything in its path and then ruptured a water main, engorging it further and increasing the speed of its descent towards the school. A survivor said later, “one minute we were young innocent children of eight years of age … and then at twenty past nine we were totally different people and would never be the same again.” I have decided to leave most of the witness testimony out of this assembly. One of the first police officers on the scene recalls being rigid with shock. "A huge bank of water was coming directly towards us," she said. "It was like a tsunami, it was terrifying”. The crisis whistle sounded in the colliery and miners, their headlamps still lit, ran to the school where women were clawing at the slurry trying in vain to reach the children. News reports described the site resembling an earthquake or the aftermath of a high explosive bomb. I can’t tell you what the parents went through, but one rescuer recalled: “It goes to show how primitive it all seems; I wrote up a notice and pinned it to the chapel door informing parents that death certificates will be issued at the local fish and chip shop”. The waiting took 15 days to identify 144 bodies. The handful of surviving children did not really have a formal education for many years. Time and again, testimonies from the past describe the same thing – no one talked about what happened. This was an age of a stiff upper lip, embodied by the tough, macho miners themselves. Psychological help was stigmatised and viewed with suspicion. A local GP described the village as consumed with guilt, psychological problems, alcoholism and nervous breakdowns. All of that went untreated. What followed was a saga of cruelty and indignity. Donations to the Aberfan Disaster Fund poured in from all over the world but the money was taken away and the bereaved were initially refused help to pay for their children’s gravestones. The Coal Board initially offered £50 of compensation for each dead child before raising it to the "generous offer" of £500. A more substantial sum, it was advised, would have destroyed the working-class recipients not used to large amounts of money. The NCB chairman insisted to reporters that it was “impossible to know that there was a spring in the heart of this tip” although everyone else seemed to know and Ordnance Survey maps proved it. The tribunal that followed concluded the disaster was “a terrifying tale of bungling ineptitude by many men charged with tasks for which they were totally unfitted, of failure to heed clear warnings, and of a total lack of direction from above”. No one lost their jobs, was demoted or fined. This is obviously a horrible story. I’m telling you because you need to know, and it’s an antidote to thinking that Britain was such a brilliant place in the past. I could have chosen any number of examples. The 70s, 80s and 90s featured behaviour and events that I can scarcely believe are true from today’s perspective. And of course, the main reason I’m telling you is because you represent the Britain of the future. We won’t move forwards by nostalgic memories of some phoney past. As future leaders and people who will serve our communities, it’s your job to present an attractive vision of a better society that we can all work towards. Our speaker at prizegiving, Chanel Contos, was an inspiring example of a youthful changemaker. And the obvious first step is for you to be the change you want to see in the world.

### [Prizegiving Speaker and Australian Activist Chanel Contos, Inspires Pupils](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/prizegiving-speaker-and-australian-activist-chanel-contos-inspires-pupils)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 9, 2026

On Friday 4 September, we were honoured to welcome Chanel Contos as guest speaker for Prizegiving 2026. Chanel is an Australian activist and Founder of Teach Us Consent, she was also the recipient of the Australian Human Rights Commission Young People’s Medal in 2021, and in 2023 she was named NSW Young Woman of the Year for her persistent efforts towards eradicating rape culture. Chanel has worked with Norwich School twice in the past, it was an honour to have her back in Cathedral Close. You can read her address below; It's an absolute honour to be here with you all tonight and to have been asked to present your prizes. I’ve visited Norwich a few times now and this school has a special place in my heart as every time I have come I’ve had conversations with students who inspire me and leave me in awe of their ability to discuss complicated topics of the world around them with such grace. When I was 15, my peers and I were taught what consent was for the first time. To this day, I found it the most valuable single lesson I ever received at school. We had a collective realisation as a year group, that almost every one one of us had either been, or had a close friend who had been sexually assaulted. The reason that my consent education talk was so mind-blowing, was because these behaviours that constitute indecent assault, sexual assault, and rape were so incredibly pervasive, that we didn’t even recognise them as an anomaly. After the talk, my friends and I went to see our head of senior school to give feedback. We had never ventured into a teacher’s office at lunchtime to tell them our thoughts on the curriculum, so that’s indicative of how passionate we were. We told her that the talk was incredible, but we had been taught it too late. With all good intentions, she explained that it’s hard enough to get a talk about consent approved by Year 10 parents, when most of the students are 16. We leave disheartened and move on quickly, but we keep having conversations amongst ourselves well into adulthood about these topics. I like to think of this as the beginning of my journey advocating for consent education. My school had the ability to deliver this education to us because we were a private school and had the flexibility to work outside of the school curriculum, but I wanted it to be taught earlier, and I wanted everyone to have access to this incredibly important information. Fast forward 8 years, and in 2021 and admittedly during a moment of extreme anger, I started Teach Us Consent by posting an instagram story asking people to submit testimonies of their own sexual assaults, naming the school they went to, the school their perpetrator went to and their graduating years. I requested that people avoid using any identifying information as I had no intention of singling out individuals. It was not simply about the fact that this happened – it was about that it happened to most of us. This was pivotal to Teach Us Consent’s founding ethos: be ruthless with systems, but kind to the people in them. This way of activism has worked for me as I can always be true to myself and speak truth to power, but never scapegoat or isolate individuals in the mission towards eradiating sexual violence, where we all have a role to play. I collected and published over 6700 testimonies, and 50,000 people signed my petition for consent education to be taught in schools. After a year of campaigning, I presented at a meeting with all Ministers of Education around the country, and they unanimously agreed to mandate consent education in all Australian schools every year, from Kindergarten, until year 10. Now, Teach Us Consent is a government-funded charity with 12 full time employees, and we’ve contributed to multiple policy and law changes in Australia. This was something I am super proud of, but tonight we are here to celebrate your achievements. You've all worked hard. You've excelled academically, creatively, athletically, musically, or through the contribution you've made to your school community. You should be incredibly proud of that, and it’s a privilege to be here with you tonight to celebrate and congratulate you. I have no doubt you’ll all go on to have many other recognitions and achievements in your life, but your biggest achievements may never appear on a transcript or manifest as a prize. Some of the most important things you’ll ever do may be noticing that something everyone else accepts as normal isn’t actually right. Your proudest moments should come from how you conduct yourself amongst friends, family or when no one is watching. Consistency to your morals and passions may not be celebrated in a big moment like today, but it’ll be noticed by those around you every day, and in yourself always. I want to leave you with a final reflection about your age. It may feel like being young is a disadvantage when you’re trying to make change or achieve things, because many people act like it is, but it’s actually a superpower and you mustn’t let others dismiss your experience of the world. Young people are often closest to the experiences that decision makers are trying to shape. You're living through the culture that adults are discussing on the news. You're using the technology that older people are trying to regulate and you're experiencing the education systems we're designing. I'm very often the youngest person in the room - in meetings with politicians, at conferences, events and convenings. I think our blissful ignorance about how system and structures are ‘meant’ to work can be exactly what helps us disrupt them. And, ultimately, you're the ones who are going to live out the policies and decisions that people in those rooms are making today. I'm now 28, and that means I’m too old to be the youngest person in the room. I don’t even use snapchat anymore. We need young people asking questions that older people might not think to ask. We need young people saying, "Actually, that's not how it feels for us, this is." So to the prize winners here tonight: you don't need to wait until you have the qualifications, the job title, the experience or the permission. I was 22 and posted an Instagram story from my bedroom that resulted in the biggest education policy change Australia has ever had. I am confident the biggest things and most important things you will ever do haven't happened yet, but maybe the ideas for them have come from your time at Norwich, or the problems you’ve identified have come from being a young person, and realising that the ‘adults’ aren’t paying close enough attention to your needs, or aware of solutions. Congratulations to every prize winner tonight, and to your parents, teachers and everyone who has helped you get here. Education is supposed to be a human right, but unfortunately it is still a privilage, so please do all you can with the opportunites your parents and teachers have given you. You should be extremely proud of yourselves, I am definitely proud of you. And I hope that, in the years ahead, you give yourselves permission not only to succeed in the world as it is, but to change the parts of it that you think need changing.

By Eleanor Lewis•September 3, 2026

Welcome to the Cathedral or welcome back to the Cathedral. Whether this is your first school service or not, it is great to have the whole senior school community together in this extraordinary building – how lucky we are to gather here. I very much enjoyed meeting our new pupils at the various induction events yesterday and am grateful to all in the community who helped to make these events successful. As you would expect, we talked about the importance of settling in and feeling that you belong. As I now widen this welcome to the rest of the senior school, I echo the same message and observe that part of settling is identifying and aiming for targets during the coming year. Whether it be connected to academic work, sport, music, performing arts, community service, outdoor education or a particular club or society, there will be numerous things you want to achieve this year. I wonder what has shaped this ambition. Because whether you are a new or returning pupil, there will be context for each of you. The start of a new school year is a glorious opportunity, a blank page on which to create the next part of your life journey. However, it cannot be the first page, even for our new L4. We are shaped by long-term factors such as home life, but we are also shaped by more immediate factors such as holiday reading, recent trips and things we have seen. Some of what I want to say today came from a summer visit to an exhibition at the Sainsbury Centre, part of the UEA, more of which later. So a key question becomes, “Where have you come from and where are you going?” And while there will be many answers to the first part of this question as the new year starts, I am afraid that there is no opt-out to the second part; you have no choice but to engage. This is not because of school but because of the world around us. It is changing fast and it is coming at you; it is not waiting for you to emerge from school to stroll into your chosen career. You have to be using us to build up your skills and interests so that you are ready for the world beyond school. An obvious example is AI. There is no doubt that AI will be important in your period of active work during and after school, but what is increasingly clear is that the power-brokers will be those who know how to harness its power within a moral, historical and cultural framework; put another way, learning how to ask the right questions and make appropriate use of the answers. A related area is around information and knowledge: It is true that the modern world has a lot of information available at the press of the button, but the most successful users of this facility will be those who have read broadly and deeply enough to have their own hinterland of knowledge, a curated facility for imagination and experience of an open-minded approach to make exciting connections with new information. To expand on this theme of world readiness, the development of genuine interests, the creation of areas of expertise and the practising of interpersonal skills are emerging as being at least as important as paper qualifications. Results are often needed to get in the door, to get the in-person interview, but the clincher in getting the role, the internship or the work experience is the warm personality you show, the adaptability to changing circumstances that you can evidence, the creativity to solve a problem, the collaborative spirit to involve others in a shared endeavour. Norvicensians can take on this challenge with great confidence: the strength of our community is authentic and sincere, so you can practise everything on the above list while you are with us. However, to do so, you need to involve yourself; hence the invitation earlier to think about what your targets are for the year. It means that events like the Clubs and Societies Fair next Tuesday are very important for everyone here, whether you are new or not. That will give you the chance to get involved in various opportunities so that you can be developing your personal portfolio and practising the skills you will need both during and after your Norwich School careers. And there is an important motivator for getting stuck into the breadth of opportunity available in Cathedral Close other than utility for later life. It is fun! The Sainsbury Centre exhibition to which I referred earlier is called Play Power. Its introduction states the following: “Showcasing a variety of manifestations of play, both past and present, ranging from board games, games of chance, physical activity, creativity, video games and make believe, as well as ritual gambling and divination, the exhibition highlights the enduring role of play in shaping human societies”. I commend the exhibition to you and also encourage you to find opportunities to play. As the exhibition shows, play has been part of different societies throughout history because play gives us the chance to learn about ourselves and others in a safe space. Play is not just having a break from the serious stuff; it may just be creating the extra, magic ingredient to shape your life in the future. To conclude, much of what I have said so far has been about individual development: building up critical judgment and improving your reading portfolio as part of your intellectual development; taking opportunities to learn and be creative through play in our clubs and societies programme. Yet many of the 21st century skills I referenced earlier were relational: collaboration, adaptability, teamwork. And this is where perhaps the biggest jewel in the Norwich School crown can be found: the community itself. Because we care about each other, because both peer and teacher-pupil relationships are so strong, you can commit fully to getting involved with the confidence that any such efforts will be welcomed and supported. Here, you will be able, indeed expected, to practise being kind, showing humility and working with others. All these behaviours build up the gentle self-confidence and desire to be a force for good that are the hallmarks of our best Norvicensians. I encourage you not to take the quality of our community for granted but to make the most of it. In my experience, it is not normal for educational settings to be so thoughtful, positive and supportive; it is a culture that needs to be nurtured, practised and celebrated. With all that I have said today, there is a significant overlap with today’s bible reading: “never be lacking in zeal…Live in harmony with one another…Do not be conceited…Be careful to do what is right in the eyes of everyone…”. In the light of our outstanding public examination results, where so many of our new L6 and departing U6 performed right at the top of expectations, I finish with a call-to-arms about the importance of a positive attitude. It is a quote from the industrialist, Henry Ford: “Whether you think you can or you think you can’t, you’re right”. Have a great first day of term; I look forward to observing you “thinking that you can” around school!

Where they are **supported, celebrated and pushed forward** by each other.

Where they can **speak up** without fear of judgement – **play** without fear of ridicule – **learn without limits**.

## Why girls only?

**Girls and boys are equal – but they’re not the same**. How they grow and learn is different.

Evidence suggests that in a girls only school, girls:

*   are less likely to conform to gender stereotypes,
*   are less constrained in their subject choices,
*   show a greater propensity to take risks and innovate,
*   perform better in exams,
*   have more opportunities to show leadership, and
*   are more successful in the job market.

Here at the only all-girls private school in Norwich, girls are given every opportunity, without prejudice, to **explore and fulfil their potential**.

Choosing an independent girls’ school like Norwich High School For Girls means providing an education that’s tailored to how girls learn best, at every stage—from [nursery](https://www.norwichhigh.gdst.net/early-years/welcome/) and [prep](https://www.norwichhigh.gdst.net/prep-school/welcome/), to [senior school](https://www.norwichhigh.gdst.net/senior-school/welcome/), [sixth form](https://www.norwichhigh.gdst.net/sixth-form/welcome/) and beyond.

**Girls and boys are equal – but they’re not the same**. How they grow and learn is different.

## Norwich School is a co-educational,independent day school

Norwich School is an independent, co-educational day school for pupils aged between three and eighteen.

Set in the beautiful grounds of the city’s historic Cathedral Close, the school is a traditional yet lively place to learn and combines a vibrant, imaginative culture with values of scholarship and mutual respect.

### [Summer of Cricket Success](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/summer-of-cricket-success)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 15, 2026

It has been a fantastic summer of cricket, with several strong performances across the Norfolk County age group programme and some notable achievements involving members of the Norwich school community. Our 1st XI captain represented the Norfolk Lions against Suffolk 2nd XI while Lucas B, Max C, Charlie M, Vihaan R, Jaivir A, William J, Freddie P, and Josh B all represented the Norfolk boys age-group squads with success. In the girl’s programme, Isobel S continued her run-scoring form with two more centuries while Charlotte P, Lucy H, Orla B, Georgina D, Rosie B and Bella L alongside On’s India Fox and Niamh Rushton enjoyed excellent season for representing Norfolk. Bella B was selected for an England schools U17 squad that competed in the National school’s competition against Ireland and Scotland where they were crowned eventual winners of the Ebony Rainford-Brent T20 trophy, a fantastic achievement. Our cricket staff also enjoyed an outstanding summer with Mr Alfie Cooper, current Swardeston CC captain, earned his Norfolk County Cricket cap and finished as the leading Minor counties run scorer in the three-day format, that included two centuries. Meanwhile, Mr Richard Sims, our 1st XI Girl’s coach, represented England over-40’s in their Triple Crown competition against Wales, Scotland and Ireland. We wish Mr Sims every success as he travels to Guyana in late October to represent England over-40’s in the World Cup. It has been a memorable summer for the Norwich school cricket programme, and certainly one to celebrate.

### [Ways into the Cathedral - an Address from Rev Child](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/ways-into-the-cathedral-an-address-from-rev-child)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 11, 2026

I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let us go to the house of the Lord!’ (Psalm 122:1) We’ve been in the cathedral a fair bit since term started. I want to start with a question for you to think about, whether you’re new here or whether you’ve been around for a while: How many different ways into the cathedral do you think there are? When you came in this morning, you had a choice of two doorways – the two west corners at the back. On the first day of term, for a bit of pomp and ceremony, we opened the main west doors to allow a procession in and out. There are other ways in through the gift shop; or through the north or south transepts. All the way up at the east end there’s a door that leads from Edith Cavell’s grave outside to the inside of the military chapel. There used to be a suspended walkway from upstairs in the Bishop’s Palace across to the first floor level in here to save the bishop getting rained on. I’m actually not sure myself how many ways into Norwich Cathedral there are now. If you know the answer – or if at some point you have a spare ten minutes to walk round the building counting the doorways – perhaps you could let me know. Many years ago, before I lived and worked in Norwich, before I was even a priest, I visited Norwich Cathedral with a group of year 6 children from South London. They were in Norfolk on their week-long school journey to experience something different to their usual. I don’t remember which door we came in that day. But I do remember that I was a bit concerned about one of the pupils in the group. His name was Daniel. He was the naughty one. I was worried he was going to find the cathedral boring and start messing around. As it turned out, I was completely wrong. We started our tour in the cloisters – the outdoors space on the south side surrounded by walkways and pillars. Our guide was a retired teacher who guessed that, before we saw the stained glass windows or the bishop’s cathedra, we might like to see a game played by the monks who originally lived here. It was a very simple game – the monks would stand on the ledges in the cloisters and swing round the pillars like apes. (We know that they did this because their feet wore grooves into the stone that you can still see today.) Our guide had already spotted Daniel, and he asked him to demonstrate swinging round the pillars. Sure enough, Daniel’s feet naturally fitted into the grooves as he moved. From that moment, he was fascinated. I think partly because he simply wasn’t expecting there to be fun in the cathedral. But with the help of the guide, Daniel found his own way into this place. Later we were shown some hidden medieval graffiti. Right in the middle of it we happened to find Daniel’s initials, carved by someone centuries ago. It was wonderful to watch Daniel feeling like he belonged here. However many literal doorways there are, I hope you can all find your own figurative way into this cathedral. If you have some kind of a maths brain, the physics and the proportions around us are extraordinary. A while ago Dr Leeder gave an assembly on how many Smarties you can fit in this space. Let the numbers inspire you. If you’re someone who likes Art and Design, there’s no shortage of craftmanship in here that you can get up close to. It’s not all in the past; even today you might see a modern stonemason winching a block of stone up the scaffolding outside to repair centuries of rain and wind erosion. Be inspired by the necessary work of people who are really good at 3D Design. If you’ve just started a course in Psychology, ask yourself why human beings are motivated to begin buildings like this in the first place. The first ever Bishop of Norwich, buried at the east end, was consumed by shame and guilt; he began the construction of this cathedral as a penance. Just about everything we teach is represented: languages, like Latin and a little Anglo-Norman; or poetry, written on the walls; or music, of course; or history, in bucketloads. It’s all here, waiting for you to spot something that catches your interest, and which will take you further in. What is generally true in education is true here: there are many ways in. Just choose your doorway. I want to close by reading part of an email that I got from an ON recently. This is someone who has been away from Norwich School for two decades and now lives in Australia; these are his recollections. Looking back, it is quite remarkable that a load of teenagers meet in the cathedral in the morning… I barely noticed how unusual this was at the time, but the very act of starting the day within an enormous, time-tested cathedral and singing together has by itself a very unifying and edifying effect. When catching up with my peers occasionally, one repeated theme that emerges is how we miss the sense of the transcendent that pervaded school life in the cathedral close. It's so easy to become busied up with urban life and work… longing for meaning and fullness and forgetting where it comes from. You may know that on this date 25 years ago – the 11th September 2001, or 9/11 – there was an attack on the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon in Washington which sent shock waves around the globe. We keep this anniversary in mind as we come to our prayer for this morning, which is the Benedictine Prayer for Peace. Benedictine prayer for peace We would like to be people of peace; to walk the paths of peace our whole life long, and to lead others into the ways of peace. May there be peace in our hearts, peace in our homes, peace in our sorely troubled world. May we be peace-makers, ready to take the first step in ending bitterness, being the first to hold out our hands in friendship and forgiveness. May peace, grace and love permeate our daily living. In the fullness of time, may we know the reward of being peacemakers.

### [Tom White Addresses Pupils on Aspiring Towards a Brighter Future](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/tom-white-addresses-pupils-on-aspiring-towards-a-brighter-future)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 9, 2026

I'm wearing my Make America Great Again hats today and you will be forming an opinion of what that represents. Costume is very powerful, and a MAGA hat is almost like a flag. I don't know, I must try to be balanced, and there might be Donald Trump fans in your family. In social situations, I signal my hostility to MAGA with a frown. Can I recommend that to you? When you are part of a conversation that you know is unkind, don't be a bystander. Very often a frown is a powerful and effective response that sends a very clear signal without provoking a bigger argument. It’s called frown power. Maybe we should put the ‘Great’ back into Britain. That’s a gentle joke on the people who say that sort of thing, since it indicates that they don't know what Great Britain means. Excuse me a moment while I explain. There is a large group of about 150 inhabited islands off the coast of northwestern Europe. Collectively they are called the British Isles. There are two big ones: the one on the left(west) is called Ireland. The one on the right is called Great Britain, because it is the biggest of the British Isles. This morning you are resident in a country called the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Great Britain isn't going to stop being Great anytime soon. My assembly today aims to encourage you to imagine an even better Britain: not by looking back into an imagined past, but to inspire you to work towards a future version that's even better than the present, or the past. Today I have a dreadful story to tell you about a disaster in Wales that took place almost exactly 60 years ago. Just because quite a lot of things are bad now, it doesn’t mean that everything is getting worse, or that things used to better. Things that are normal today: health and safety, counselling, accountability, litigation, compensation – were almost completely absent 60 years ago. I’m 56, so while 60 years ago sounds like ancient history if you are 12, it isn’t all that long ago in reality. On that dreadful day in October 1966, it had been raining hard for weeks. The 240 pupils of the Aberfan Junior School wound their way through the back lanes of miners’ terrace houses on their way to morning assembly. You probably know that coal mining built industrial Britain. But by 1966, the coal industry had been in long decline and several pits had shut. The mining workforce had fallen from its peak, but pit jobs kept Aberfan going. The National Coal Board had control of UK mining and wielded great power. It had a firm grip on government, and it was held in what now seems uncomfortable reverence. The working man knew his place; authority knew best. Numerous complaints had been made to the Coal Board about the dangers of one of the seven gigantic spoil tips that loomed high above the village. Every mining community had its tips of waste material dug from the mines. The entire south Wales valleys landscape was jagged with them. The one above Aberfan had slipped three years previously when an ominous crater appeared at the top. A bulge had formed at the foot of the tip as a stream that was unable to drain away liquefied the tip into thick, black quicksand. The Coal Board brushed the complaints aside. Everyone knew that if they made a fuss, the mine would be closed. If the disaster had come 20 minutes earlier, the junior school below the tip would have been empty. In the classrooms lights began to flicker and sway before there was an ominous roar. A glistening black avalanche consumed everything in its path and then ruptured a water main, engorging it further and increasing the speed of its descent towards the school. A survivor said later, “one minute we were young innocent children of eight years of age … and then at twenty past nine we were totally different people and would never be the same again.” I have decided to leave most of the witness testimony out of this assembly. One of the first police officers on the scene recalls being rigid with shock. "A huge bank of water was coming directly towards us," she said. "It was like a tsunami, it was terrifying”. The crisis whistle sounded in the colliery and miners, their headlamps still lit, ran to the school where women were clawing at the slurry trying in vain to reach the children. News reports described the site resembling an earthquake or the aftermath of a high explosive bomb. I can’t tell you what the parents went through, but one rescuer recalled: “It goes to show how primitive it all seems; I wrote up a notice and pinned it to the chapel door informing parents that death certificates will be issued at the local fish and chip shop”. The waiting took 15 days to identify 144 bodies. The handful of surviving children did not really have a formal education for many years. Time and again, testimonies from the past describe the same thing – no one talked about what happened. This was an age of a stiff upper lip, embodied by the tough, macho miners themselves. Psychological help was stigmatised and viewed with suspicion. A local GP described the village as consumed with guilt, psychological problems, alcoholism and nervous breakdowns. All of that went untreated. What followed was a saga of cruelty and indignity. Donations to the Aberfan Disaster Fund poured in from all over the world but the money was taken away and the bereaved were initially refused help to pay for their children’s gravestones. The Coal Board initially offered £50 of compensation for each dead child before raising it to the "generous offer" of £500. A more substantial sum, it was advised, would have destroyed the working-class recipients not used to large amounts of money. The NCB chairman insisted to reporters that it was “impossible to know that there was a spring in the heart of this tip” although everyone else seemed to know and Ordnance Survey maps proved it. The tribunal that followed concluded the disaster was “a terrifying tale of bungling ineptitude by many men charged with tasks for which they were totally unfitted, of failure to heed clear warnings, and of a total lack of direction from above”. No one lost their jobs, was demoted or fined. This is obviously a horrible story. I’m telling you because you need to know, and it’s an antidote to thinking that Britain was such a brilliant place in the past. I could have chosen any number of examples. The 70s, 80s and 90s featured behaviour and events that I can scarcely believe are true from today’s perspective. And of course, the main reason I’m telling you is because you represent the Britain of the future. We won’t move forwards by nostalgic memories of some phoney past. As future leaders and people who will serve our communities, it’s your job to present an attractive vision of a better society that we can all work towards. Our speaker at prizegiving, Chanel Contos, was an inspiring example of a youthful changemaker. And the obvious first step is for you to be the change you want to see in the world.

### [Prizegiving Speaker and Australian Activist Chanel Contos, Inspires Pupils](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/prizegiving-speaker-and-australian-activist-chanel-contos-inspires-pupils)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 9, 2026

On Friday 4 September, we were honoured to welcome Chanel Contos as guest speaker for Prizegiving 2026. Chanel is an Australian activist and Founder of Teach Us Consent, she was also the recipient of the Australian Human Rights Commission Young People’s Medal in 2021, and in 2023 she was named NSW Young Woman of the Year for her persistent efforts towards eradicating rape culture. Chanel has worked with Norwich School twice in the past, it was an honour to have her back in Cathedral Close. You can read her address below; It's an absolute honour to be here with you all tonight and to have been asked to present your prizes. I’ve visited Norwich a few times now and this school has a special place in my heart as every time I have come I’ve had conversations with students who inspire me and leave me in awe of their ability to discuss complicated topics of the world around them with such grace. When I was 15, my peers and I were taught what consent was for the first time. To this day, I found it the most valuable single lesson I ever received at school. We had a collective realisation as a year group, that almost every one one of us had either been, or had a close friend who had been sexually assaulted. The reason that my consent education talk was so mind-blowing, was because these behaviours that constitute indecent assault, sexual assault, and rape were so incredibly pervasive, that we didn’t even recognise them as an anomaly. After the talk, my friends and I went to see our head of senior school to give feedback. We had never ventured into a teacher’s office at lunchtime to tell them our thoughts on the curriculum, so that’s indicative of how passionate we were. We told her that the talk was incredible, but we had been taught it too late. With all good intentions, she explained that it’s hard enough to get a talk about consent approved by Year 10 parents, when most of the students are 16. We leave disheartened and move on quickly, but we keep having conversations amongst ourselves well into adulthood about these topics. I like to think of this as the beginning of my journey advocating for consent education. My school had the ability to deliver this education to us because we were a private school and had the flexibility to work outside of the school curriculum, but I wanted it to be taught earlier, and I wanted everyone to have access to this incredibly important information. Fast forward 8 years, and in 2021 and admittedly during a moment of extreme anger, I started Teach Us Consent by posting an instagram story asking people to submit testimonies of their own sexual assaults, naming the school they went to, the school their perpetrator went to and their graduating years. I requested that people avoid using any identifying information as I had no intention of singling out individuals. It was not simply about the fact that this happened – it was about that it happened to most of us. This was pivotal to Teach Us Consent’s founding ethos: be ruthless with systems, but kind to the people in them. This way of activism has worked for me as I can always be true to myself and speak truth to power, but never scapegoat or isolate individuals in the mission towards eradiating sexual violence, where we all have a role to play. I collected and published over 6700 testimonies, and 50,000 people signed my petition for consent education to be taught in schools. After a year of campaigning, I presented at a meeting with all Ministers of Education around the country, and they unanimously agreed to mandate consent education in all Australian schools every year, from Kindergarten, until year 10. Now, Teach Us Consent is a government-funded charity with 12 full time employees, and we’ve contributed to multiple policy and law changes in Australia. This was something I am super proud of, but tonight we are here to celebrate your achievements. You've all worked hard. You've excelled academically, creatively, athletically, musically, or through the contribution you've made to your school community. You should be incredibly proud of that, and it’s a privilege to be here with you tonight to celebrate and congratulate you. I have no doubt you’ll all go on to have many other recognitions and achievements in your life, but your biggest achievements may never appear on a transcript or manifest as a prize. Some of the most important things you’ll ever do may be noticing that something everyone else accepts as normal isn’t actually right. Your proudest moments should come from how you conduct yourself amongst friends, family or when no one is watching. Consistency to your morals and passions may not be celebrated in a big moment like today, but it’ll be noticed by those around you every day, and in yourself always. I want to leave you with a final reflection about your age. It may feel like being young is a disadvantage when you’re trying to make change or achieve things, because many people act like it is, but it’s actually a superpower and you mustn’t let others dismiss your experience of the world. Young people are often closest to the experiences that decision makers are trying to shape. You're living through the culture that adults are discussing on the news. You're using the technology that older people are trying to regulate and you're experiencing the education systems we're designing. I'm very often the youngest person in the room - in meetings with politicians, at conferences, events and convenings. I think our blissful ignorance about how system and structures are ‘meant’ to work can be exactly what helps us disrupt them. And, ultimately, you're the ones who are going to live out the policies and decisions that people in those rooms are making today. I'm now 28, and that means I’m too old to be the youngest person in the room. I don’t even use snapchat anymore. We need young people asking questions that older people might not think to ask. We need young people saying, "Actually, that's not how it feels for us, this is." So to the prize winners here tonight: you don't need to wait until you have the qualifications, the job title, the experience or the permission. I was 22 and posted an Instagram story from my bedroom that resulted in the biggest education policy change Australia has ever had. I am confident the biggest things and most important things you will ever do haven't happened yet, but maybe the ideas for them have come from your time at Norwich, or the problems you’ve identified have come from being a young person, and realising that the ‘adults’ aren’t paying close enough attention to your needs, or aware of solutions. Congratulations to every prize winner tonight, and to your parents, teachers and everyone who has helped you get here. Education is supposed to be a human right, but unfortunately it is still a privilage, so please do all you can with the opportunites your parents and teachers have given you. You should be extremely proud of yourselves, I am definitely proud of you. And I hope that, in the years ahead, you give yourselves permission not only to succeed in the world as it is, but to change the parts of it that you think need changing.

## Norwich School is a co-educational,independent day school

Norwich School is an independent, co-educational day school for pupils aged between three and eighteen.

Set in the beautiful grounds of the city’s historic Cathedral Close, the school is a traditional yet lively place to learn and combines a vibrant, imaginative culture with values of scholarship and mutual respect.

### [Ways into the Cathedral - an Address from Rev Child](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/ways-into-the-cathedral-an-address-from-rev-child)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 11, 2026

I was glad when they said to me, ‘Let us go to the house of the Lord!’ (Psalm 122:1) We’ve been in the cathedral a fair bit since term started. I want to start with a question for you to think about, whether you’re new here or whether you’ve been around for a while: How many different ways into the cathedral do you think there are? When you came in this morning, you had a choice of two doorways – the two west corners at the back. On the first day of term, for a bit of pomp and ceremony, we opened the main west doors to allow a procession in and out. There are other ways in through the gift shop; or through the north or south transepts. All the way up at the east end there’s a door that leads from Edith Cavell’s grave outside to the inside of the military chapel. There used to be a suspended walkway from upstairs in the Bishop’s Palace across to the first floor level in here to save the bishop getting rained on. I’m actually not sure myself how many ways into Norwich Cathedral there are now. If you know the answer – or if at some point you have a spare ten minutes to walk round the building counting the doorways – perhaps you could let me know. Many years ago, before I lived and worked in Norwich, before I was even a priest, I visited Norwich Cathedral with a group of year 6 children from South London. They were in Norfolk on their week-long school journey to experience something different to their usual. I don’t remember which door we came in that day. But I do remember that I was a bit concerned about one of the pupils in the group. His name was Daniel. He was the naughty one. I was worried he was going to find the cathedral boring and start messing around. As it turned out, I was completely wrong. We started our tour in the cloisters – the outdoors space on the south side surrounded by walkways and pillars. Our guide was a retired teacher who guessed that, before we saw the stained glass windows or the bishop’s cathedra, we might like to see a game played by the monks who originally lived here. It was a very simple game – the monks would stand on the ledges in the cloisters and swing round the pillars like apes. (We know that they did this because their feet wore grooves into the stone that you can still see today.) Our guide had already spotted Daniel, and he asked him to demonstrate swinging round the pillars. Sure enough, Daniel’s feet naturally fitted into the grooves as he moved. From that moment, he was fascinated. I think partly because he simply wasn’t expecting there to be fun in the cathedral. But with the help of the guide, Daniel found his own way into this place. Later we were shown some hidden medieval graffiti. Right in the middle of it we happened to find Daniel’s initials, carved by someone centuries ago. It was wonderful to watch Daniel feeling like he belonged here. However many literal doorways there are, I hope you can all find your own figurative way into this cathedral. If you have some kind of a maths brain, the physics and the proportions around us are extraordinary. A while ago Dr Leeder gave an assembly on how many Smarties you can fit in this space. Let the numbers inspire you. If you’re someone who likes Art and Design, there’s no shortage of craftmanship in here that you can get up close to. It’s not all in the past; even today you might see a modern stonemason winching a block of stone up the scaffolding outside to repair centuries of rain and wind erosion. Be inspired by the necessary work of people who are really good at 3D Design. If you’ve just started a course in Psychology, ask yourself why human beings are motivated to begin buildings like this in the first place. The first ever Bishop of Norwich, buried at the east end, was consumed by shame and guilt; he began the construction of this cathedral as a penance. Just about everything we teach is represented: languages, like Latin and a little Anglo-Norman; or poetry, written on the walls; or music, of course; or history, in bucketloads. It’s all here, waiting for you to spot something that catches your interest, and which will take you further in. What is generally true in education is true here: there are many ways in. Just choose your doorway. I want to close by reading part of an email that I got from an ON recently. This is someone who has been away from Norwich School for two decades and now lives in Australia; these are his recollections. Looking back, it is quite remarkable that a load of teenagers meet in the cathedral in the morning… I barely noticed how unusual this was at the time, but the very act of starting the day within an enormous, time-tested cathedral and singing together has by itself a very unifying and edifying effect. When catching up with my peers occasionally, one repeated theme that emerges is how we miss the sense of the transcendent that pervaded school life in the cathedral close. It's so easy to become busied up with urban life and work… longing for meaning and fullness and forgetting where it comes from. You may know that on this date 25 years ago – the 11th September 2001, or 9/11 – there was an attack on the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon in Washington which sent shock waves around the globe. We keep this anniversary in mind as we come to our prayer for this morning, which is the Benedictine Prayer for Peace. Benedictine prayer for peace We would like to be people of peace; to walk the paths of peace our whole life long, and to lead others into the ways of peace. May there be peace in our hearts, peace in our homes, peace in our sorely troubled world. May we be peace-makers, ready to take the first step in ending bitterness, being the first to hold out our hands in friendship and forgiveness. May peace, grace and love permeate our daily living. In the fullness of time, may we know the reward of being peacemakers.

### [Tom White Addresses Pupils on Aspiring Towards a Brighter Future](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/tom-white-addresses-pupils-on-aspiring-towards-a-brighter-future)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 9, 2026

I'm wearing my Make America Great Again hats today and you will be forming an opinion of what that represents. Costume is very powerful, and a MAGA hat is almost like a flag. I don't know, I must try to be balanced, and there might be Donald Trump fans in your family. In social situations, I signal my hostility to MAGA with a frown. Can I recommend that to you? When you are part of a conversation that you know is unkind, don't be a bystander. Very often a frown is a powerful and effective response that sends a very clear signal without provoking a bigger argument. It’s called frown power. Maybe we should put the ‘Great’ back into Britain. That’s a gentle joke on the people who say that sort of thing, since it indicates that they don't know what Great Britain means. Excuse me a moment while I explain. There is a large group of about 150 inhabited islands off the coast of northwestern Europe. Collectively they are called the British Isles. There are two big ones: the one on the left(west) is called Ireland. The one on the right is called Great Britain, because it is the biggest of the British Isles. This morning you are resident in a country called the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Great Britain isn't going to stop being Great anytime soon. My assembly today aims to encourage you to imagine an even better Britain: not by looking back into an imagined past, but to inspire you to work towards a future version that's even better than the present, or the past. Today I have a dreadful story to tell you about a disaster in Wales that took place almost exactly 60 years ago. Just because quite a lot of things are bad now, it doesn’t mean that everything is getting worse, or that things used to better. Things that are normal today: health and safety, counselling, accountability, litigation, compensation – were almost completely absent 60 years ago. I’m 56, so while 60 years ago sounds like ancient history if you are 12, it isn’t all that long ago in reality. On that dreadful day in October 1966, it had been raining hard for weeks. The 240 pupils of the Aberfan Junior School wound their way through the back lanes of miners’ terrace houses on their way to morning assembly. You probably know that coal mining built industrial Britain. But by 1966, the coal industry had been in long decline and several pits had shut. The mining workforce had fallen from its peak, but pit jobs kept Aberfan going. The National Coal Board had control of UK mining and wielded great power. It had a firm grip on government, and it was held in what now seems uncomfortable reverence. The working man knew his place; authority knew best. Numerous complaints had been made to the Coal Board about the dangers of one of the seven gigantic spoil tips that loomed high above the village. Every mining community had its tips of waste material dug from the mines. The entire south Wales valleys landscape was jagged with them. The one above Aberfan had slipped three years previously when an ominous crater appeared at the top. A bulge had formed at the foot of the tip as a stream that was unable to drain away liquefied the tip into thick, black quicksand. The Coal Board brushed the complaints aside. Everyone knew that if they made a fuss, the mine would be closed. If the disaster had come 20 minutes earlier, the junior school below the tip would have been empty. In the classrooms lights began to flicker and sway before there was an ominous roar. A glistening black avalanche consumed everything in its path and then ruptured a water main, engorging it further and increasing the speed of its descent towards the school. A survivor said later, “one minute we were young innocent children of eight years of age … and then at twenty past nine we were totally different people and would never be the same again.” I have decided to leave most of the witness testimony out of this assembly. One of the first police officers on the scene recalls being rigid with shock. "A huge bank of water was coming directly towards us," she said. "It was like a tsunami, it was terrifying”. The crisis whistle sounded in the colliery and miners, their headlamps still lit, ran to the school where women were clawing at the slurry trying in vain to reach the children. News reports described the site resembling an earthquake or the aftermath of a high explosive bomb. I can’t tell you what the parents went through, but one rescuer recalled: “It goes to show how primitive it all seems; I wrote up a notice and pinned it to the chapel door informing parents that death certificates will be issued at the local fish and chip shop”. The waiting took 15 days to identify 144 bodies. The handful of surviving children did not really have a formal education for many years. Time and again, testimonies from the past describe the same thing – no one talked about what happened. This was an age of a stiff upper lip, embodied by the tough, macho miners themselves. Psychological help was stigmatised and viewed with suspicion. A local GP described the village as consumed with guilt, psychological problems, alcoholism and nervous breakdowns. All of that went untreated. What followed was a saga of cruelty and indignity. Donations to the Aberfan Disaster Fund poured in from all over the world but the money was taken away and the bereaved were initially refused help to pay for their children’s gravestones. The Coal Board initially offered £50 of compensation for each dead child before raising it to the "generous offer" of £500. A more substantial sum, it was advised, would have destroyed the working-class recipients not used to large amounts of money. The NCB chairman insisted to reporters that it was “impossible to know that there was a spring in the heart of this tip” although everyone else seemed to know and Ordnance Survey maps proved it. The tribunal that followed concluded the disaster was “a terrifying tale of bungling ineptitude by many men charged with tasks for which they were totally unfitted, of failure to heed clear warnings, and of a total lack of direction from above”. No one lost their jobs, was demoted or fined. This is obviously a horrible story. I’m telling you because you need to know, and it’s an antidote to thinking that Britain was such a brilliant place in the past. I could have chosen any number of examples. The 70s, 80s and 90s featured behaviour and events that I can scarcely believe are true from today’s perspective. And of course, the main reason I’m telling you is because you represent the Britain of the future. We won’t move forwards by nostalgic memories of some phoney past. As future leaders and people who will serve our communities, it’s your job to present an attractive vision of a better society that we can all work towards. Our speaker at prizegiving, Chanel Contos, was an inspiring example of a youthful changemaker. And the obvious first step is for you to be the change you want to see in the world.

### [Prizegiving Speaker and Australian Activist Chanel Contos, Inspires Pupils](https://www.norwich-school.org.uk/prizegiving-speaker-and-australian-activist-chanel-contos-inspires-pupils)

By Eleanor Lewis•September 9, 2026

On Friday 4 September, we were honoured to welcome Chanel Contos as guest speaker for Prizegiving 2026. Chanel is an Australian activist and Founder of Teach Us Consent, she was also the recipient of the Australian Human Rights Commission Young People’s Medal in 2021, and in 2023 she was named NSW Young Woman of the Year for her persistent efforts towards eradicating rape culture. Chanel has worked with Norwich School twice in the past, it was an honour to have her back in Cathedral Close. You can read her address below; It's an absolute honour to be here with you all tonight and to have been asked to present your prizes. I’ve visited Norwich a few times now and this school has a special place in my heart as every time I have come I’ve had conversations with students who inspire me and leave me in awe of their ability to discuss complicated topics of the world around them with such grace. When I was 15, my peers and I were taught what consent was for the first time. To this day, I found it the most valuable single lesson I ever received at school. We had a collective realisation as a year group, that almost every one one of us had either been, or had a close friend who had been sexually assaulted. The reason that my consent education talk was so mind-blowing, was because these behaviours that constitute indecent assault, sexual assault, and rape were so incredibly pervasive, that we didn’t even recognise them as an anomaly. After the talk, my friends and I went to see our head of senior school to give feedback. We had never ventured into a teacher’s office at lunchtime to tell them our thoughts on the curriculum, so that’s indicative of how passionate we were. We told her that the talk was incredible, but we had been taught it too late. With all good intentions, she explained that it’s hard enough to get a talk about consent approved by Year 10 parents, when most of the students are 16. We leave disheartened and move on quickly, but we keep having conversations amongst ourselves well into adulthood about these topics. I like to think of this as the beginning of my journey advocating for consent education. My school had the ability to deliver this education to us because we were a private school and had the flexibility to work outside of the school curriculum, but I wanted it to be taught earlier, and I wanted everyone to have access to this incredibly important information. Fast forward 8 years, and in 2021 and admittedly during a moment of extreme anger, I started Teach Us Consent by posting an instagram story asking people to submit testimonies of their own sexual assaults, naming the school they went to, the school their perpetrator went to and their graduating years. I requested that people avoid using any identifying information as I had no intention of singling out individuals. It was not simply about the fact that this happened – it was about that it happened to most of us. This was pivotal to Teach Us Consent’s founding ethos: be ruthless with systems, but kind to the people in them. This way of activism has worked for me as I can always be true to myself and speak truth to power, but never scapegoat or isolate individuals in the mission towards eradiating sexual violence, where we all have a role to play. I collected and published over 6700 testimonies, and 50,000 people signed my petition for consent education to be taught in schools. After a year of campaigning, I presented at a meeting with all Ministers of Education around the country, and they unanimously agreed to mandate consent education in all Australian schools every year, from Kindergarten, until year 10. Now, Teach Us Consent is a government-funded charity with 12 full time employees, and we’ve contributed to multiple policy and law changes in Australia. This was something I am super proud of, but tonight we are here to celebrate your achievements. You've all worked hard. You've excelled academically, creatively, athletically, musically, or through the contribution you've made to your school community. You should be incredibly proud of that, and it’s a privilege to be here with you tonight to celebrate and congratulate you. I have no doubt you’ll all go on to have many other recognitions and achievements in your life, but your biggest achievements may never appear on a transcript or manifest as a prize. Some of the most important things you’ll ever do may be noticing that something everyone else accepts as normal isn’t actually right. Your proudest moments should come from how you conduct yourself amongst friends, family or when no one is watching. Consistency to your morals and passions may not be celebrated in a big moment like today, but it’ll be noticed by those around you every day, and in yourself always. I want to leave you with a final reflection about your age. It may feel like being young is a disadvantage when you’re trying to make change or achieve things, because many people act like it is, but it’s actually a superpower and you mustn’t let others dismiss your experience of the world. Young people are often closest to the experiences that decision makers are trying to shape. You're living through the culture that adults are discussing on the news. You're using the technology that older people are trying to regulate and you're experiencing the education systems we're designing. I'm very often the youngest person in the room - in meetings with politicians, at conferences, events and convenings. I think our blissful ignorance about how system and structures are ‘meant’ to work can be exactly what helps us disrupt them. And, ultimately, you're the ones who are going to live out the policies and decisions that people in those rooms are making today. I'm now 28, and that means I’m too old to be the youngest person in the room. I don’t even use snapchat anymore. We need young people asking questions that older people might not think to ask. We need young people saying, "Actually, that's not how it feels for us, this is." So to the prize winners here tonight: you don't need to wait until you have the qualifications, the job title, the experience or the permission. I was 22 and posted an Instagram story from my bedroom that resulted in the biggest education policy change Australia has ever had. I am confident the biggest things and most important things you will ever do haven't happened yet, but maybe the ideas for them have come from your time at Norwich, or the problems you’ve identified have come from being a young person, and realising that the ‘adults’ aren’t paying close enough attention to your needs, or aware of solutions. Congratulations to every prize winner tonight, and to your parents, teachers and everyone who has helped you get here. Education is supposed to be a human right, but unfortunately it is still a privilage, so please do all you can with the opportunites your parents and teachers have given you. You should be extremely proud of yourselves, I am definitely proud of you. And I hope that, in the years ahead, you give yourselves permission not only to succeed in the world as it is, but to change the parts of it that you think need changing.

# A Leading Independent, Inclusive Preparatory School in Norwich

Since 1864, Notre Dame Preparatory School has been a beacon of excellence, holding a proud tradition of success that permeates everything we do. We welcome [nursery](https://www.notredameprepschool.co.uk/nursery/ "Independent Nursery in Norwich, Norfolk") age children and pupils in [reception](https://www.notredameprepschool.co.uk/pre-prep/ "Independent Pre Prep School in Norwich, Norfolk") through to [Year 6](https://www.notredameprepschool.co.uk/prep/ "Independent Prep School in Norwich, Norfolk").

As a small, independent Catholic school in the heart of Norwich, children are encouraged to be curious, creative and, above all, happy. We believe learning happens when children feel safe, valued and inspired, and we place wellbeing at the entire of everything we do.

Our doors swing wide open for all, with no entrance exams or religious demands. We cherish diversity and welcome families from all faiths, or none at all. Parents speak of the close-knit community at Notre Dame Prep, a supportive environment where every child is known and celebrated. In our 2025 inspection, NDPS met all standards set by the Independent Schools Inspectorate, commenting “Pupils of all abilities engage in interesting and relevant activities, behave appropriately and make good progress in their lessons,” reinforcing our belief that we are the premier choice for children embarking on the next step of their educational journey.

The best way to learn more about our school is to visit us, and we are certain you will feel the warmth of our community once you step inside.

**Norwich High School for Girls** is a [private](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_schools_in_the_United_Kingdom "Private schools in the United Kingdom")[day school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_school "Day school") for girls aged 3 to 18 in [Norwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich,_United_Kingdom "Norwich, United Kingdom"), England. The school was founded in 1875 by the [Girls’ Public Day School Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girls'_Public_Day_School_Company "Girls' Public Day School Company") (now the [Girls' Day School Trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girls'_Day_School_Trust "Girls' Day School Trust")), which aimed to establish schools for girls of all classes by providing a high standard of academic, moral and religious education.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The school is a member of the [Girls’ Schools Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girls'_Schools_Association "Girls' Schools Association")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-1) and the [Headmasters’ and Headmistresses’ Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Headmasters'_and_Headmistresses'_Conference "Headmasters' and Headmistresses' Conference").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-2) The school consistently has one of the best academic results in East Anglia.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-3)[_[obsolete source](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:AGE\_MATTERS "Wikipedia:AGE MATTERS")_]

Entry into the school is selective at 4+, 7+, 11+, 13+ and 16+.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-4)

## History and location

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Norwich_High_School_for_Girls&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History and location")]

Norwich High School for Girls was founded in 1875 as the first [GPDST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDST "GDST") school outside London. Originally situated at the [Assembly House, Norwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_House "Assembly House"), the school moved to its present location Eaton Grove, 95 Newmarket Road in 1933.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-5) Eaton Grove is Grade II listed.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-6) The school occupies several buildings, all of which were originally private houses; Stafford House (preparatory school), Eaton Grove (senior school) and Lanchester House (sixth form).

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Norwich_High_School_for_Girls&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Year naming")]

Norwich High School uses its own nomenclature for the year groups.

**Stafford House**

*   Nursery (ages 3–4)
*   Reception (ages 4–5)
*   Kindergarten (aged 5–6)
*   Lower I (ages 6–7)
*   Upper I (ages 7–8)
*   Lower II (ages 8–9)
*   Upper II (ages 9–10)
*   Lower III (ages 10–11)

**Eaton Grove**

*   Upper III (ages 11–12)
*   Lower IV (ages 12–13)
*   Upper IV (ages 13–14)
*   Lower V (ages 14–15)
*   Upper V (ages 15–16)

**Lanchester House**

*   Lower VI - Sixth Form (ages 16–17)
*   Upper VI - Sixth Form (ages 17–18)

## School Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Norwich_High_School_for_Girls&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: School Life")]

In Upper III (Year 7) and below all pupils study a broad curriculum including Latin and two modern languages. Pupils are required to take at least nine General Certificate of Secondary Education (GCSE) and IGCSE subjects in Lower V (Year 10) and Upper V (Year 11). In the sixth form, pupils usually study four or five AS-Level subjects for one year and most continue with three subjects to A-Level. Many students take the Extended Project Qualification (EPQ). In total, there are 24 subjects offered at A-Level.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-8)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable\_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] Academically, the school is one of the highest performing independent schools in East Anglia.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-9)

## Facilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Norwich_High_School_for_Girls&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Facilities")]

The school's facilities include a sports hall, performing arts studio, main hall (including stage), junior school hall, rowing gym, outdoor theatre, lecture theatre, boardroom, 25-metre swimming pool, 13 acres of playing fields, fitness suite, 8 tennis courts and 1 astro turf.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-10)

## Scholarships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Norwich_High_School_for_Girls&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Scholarships")]

Academic scholarships and means-tested bursaries are offered upon entry to Upper III and Lower VI. The scholarships offered in Upper III are music scholarships based on the performance of the candidate in an audition and academic scholarships on their performance in the transfer or entrance to the senior school examination, whereas the scholarships offered in Lower VI are based on the performance in an optional examination based on English, Mathematics, Science and a foreign language of the candidate's choice from French, German or Spanish.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norwich_High_School_for_Girls#cite_note-11)
